name: Scenario Analysis
analogy: Think of it as a fire drill for your portfolio. You do not guess which emergency will happen; you name a few specific ones, walk through exactly what each would do to the positions you hold today, and put the results side by side.

steps.title: Write a few named stories
steps.description: You choose a small number of scenarios, each a coherent story in which several things move together. They can replay a real past episode or be a made-up shock judged plausible.
steps.inExample: Three scenarios: a central bank rate surprise, a liquidity crisis, and a quiet upward grind.

steps.title: Say how the main drivers move in each story
steps.description: Each story is defined by a few big drivers, such as the market level, volatility and spreads. The assumptions are written down so anyone can disagree with a specific one.
steps.inExample: Rate surprise: the index falls 4 percent. Liquidity crisis: the index falls 5 percent and exits cost an extra 12 points. Quiet grind: the index rises 1 percent.

steps.title: Translate driver moves into price moves
steps.description: Using known sensitivities, each driver shock is converted into a new price for every instrument held. This links a broad story to the specific contracts in the book.
steps.inExample: A 4 percent fall applied to MNQ at 19,800 moves it down by 792 points.

steps.title: Revalue the portfolio under each story
steps.description: The current positions are marked at the shocked prices, giving the profit or loss and any other risk measure, such as the share of the account lost.
steps.inExample: Five long MNQ contracts at 2 US dollars per point lose 792 times 2 times 5, or 7,920 US dollars, in the rate surprise.

steps.title: Lay the results side by side
steps.description: The output is a table with one row per scenario, showing the result next to its assumptions. It does not say which scenario will occur; it says what would happen if each did.
steps.inExample: The table shows a loss of 7,920 for the rate surprise, 10,020 for the liquidity crisis, and a gain of 1,980 for the quiet grind.

useFor.task: Daily stress review of the current book
useFor.example: Reporting what the open MNQ and ES positions would gain or lose under a replay of a past sharp sell-off.
Asking what a pairs trade between two index futures loses if their usual relationship reverses for a week.
Estimating the book's exposure to a surprise rate decision the afternoon before it is announced.

useFor.task: Working backwards from a loss limit
useFor.example: Identifying which move in the index and in volatility would produce the maximum tolerable loss, and watching for it.

avoidWhen: You need the probability of each outcome or the full range of possibilities; a Monte Carlo simulation covers the space where this method covers only the stories you thought of.
You expect the stories to predict the future; they are tools for preparing, and the real event will rarely match one.

example.scenario: Before a central bank announcement, a trader holding five long MNQ contracts at 19,800 in a 50,000 US dollar account wants to see what three named scenarios would do to the account.

input.summary: The current position and three scenarios with their assumed index moves.

fields.name: position
fields.meaning: The current holding in the book.

fields.name: reference price
fields.meaning: The MNQ price at which the scenarios are applied.

fields.name: point value
fields.meaning: What one index point is worth for one MNQ contract.

fields.name: account equity
fields.meaning: The size of the account against which losses are judged.

fields.name: rate surprise
fields.meaning: A hike that the market did not expect.

fields.name: liquidity crisis
fields.value: index down 5 percent, 12 points of extra exit slippage
fields.meaning: A fall made worse by thin order books.

fields.name: quiet grind
fields.meaning: A slow rise with low volatility.

output.summary: The profit or loss of the current position under each scenario.

fields.name: rate surprise result
fields.meaning: A fall of 792 points on 5 contracts at 2 US dollars per point.

fields.name: liquidity crisis result
fields.meaning: A fall of 990 points plus 120 US dollars of extra slippage.

fields.name: quiet grind result
fields.meaning: A rise of 198 points on 5 contracts.

fields.name: worst case share of account
fields.meaning: The liquidity crisis loss as a share of 50,000 US dollars of equity.

example.reading: The book risks about a fifth of the account in the worst story and gains only a little in the best. If a 20 percent hit is more than you accept, reduce size or add a hedge before the event, then run the same scenarios again to confirm the change.
